statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether designer benzodiazepines (benzodiazepines and close relatives sold on the illicit market, such as etizolam, clonazolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam, of which etizolam and phenazepam are licensed medicines in a few countries) are more dangerous than prescribed benzodiazepines: no source read here compares them, and neither source counts the people who used them without coming to attention, so neither gives a risk per use. In US poison-centre records (the National Poison Data System), 474 exposures to designer benzodiazepines were reported from 2014 to 2017; the 234 intentional exposures to one of 11 coded designer benzodiazepines and no other substance were analysed, while the reports involving other substances, about half, were neither collected nor analysed (Carpenter et al., 2019). The 234 were mostly etizolam (162) and clonazolam (50); the median age was 25, 86% were men, and 42 (18 in 100) were coded as suspected suicide. Drowsiness or lethargy was coded in 152 (65 in 100), slurred speech in 40 (17), confusion in 32 (14), agitation or irritability in 22 (9), a fast heart rate in 20 (9), low blood pressure in 19 (8) and coma in 10 (4), as the table gives them (the text gives 14% for agitation and 8% for coma), and 7 people (3 in 100) were intubated. Of the 224 whose care was recorded (editors' sum), 92 (41 in 100) were treated and released, 31 (14 in 100) admitted to a non-critical-care ward, 49 (22 in 100) to critical care and 36 (16 in 100) to a psychiatric facility; 9 (4 in 100) had a major effect, and one man, aged 29, died after a reported intentional ingestion of etizolam (1 of 234, 0.4%); effects lasted less than a day in 151 of the 178 with a recorded duration (85 in 100; editors' sum of the table's rows). The drug in each report is the one named by the caller and coded by poison-centre staff, with no laboratory confirmation, and the authors say people may have taken other compounds than those coded; they expect people without significant symptoms to have gone unreported, so that the reports undercount exposures and overstate severity; and a death after flubromazolam, coded under the general 'benzodiazepine' code, was missing from the data. Reports rose from 26 in 2014 to 112 in 2017, a 330% increase that the abstract reads as rising incidence, but only etizolam had its own code before 2016: etizolam alone went from 26 to 60 reports. In published case reports and forensic series up to March 2021, as compiled in a review that did not appraise them (Brunetti et al., 2021; so these figures are second-hand), 12 designer benzodiazepines appear in 141 death entries, 63 cases of impaired driving and 44 emergency admissions, from eight countries; the deaths were mostly with phenazepam (60), flualprazolam (38) and etizolam (34). By the editors' count of the review's table, 115 of the 141 death entries also list at least one opioid (methadone in 51, morphine or 6-acetylmorphine in 49), 2 more list loperamide or its metabolite, and 3 list no other drug; at least four people appear to be listed twice, all four with an opioid, and counting each of them once gives 111 of 137 (editors' calculation), about 8 in 10 either way. The two deaths in which, by the review's text, phenazepam alone was listed as the cause list alcohol in one and diazepam with dihydrocodeine in the other. In the emergency cases the review describes mostly sedation (depression of the central nervous system), and agitation and delirium in a few (editors' summary of its drug-by-drug text); its authors say that because several drugs are usually present, a death often cannot be assigned to one of them, and that blood levels overlapped between drivers judged impaired and drivers judged not impaired, and were similar in drivers and in deaths. The review's introduction says that, compared with classical benzodiazepines, these drugs produce strong sedation and amnesia and raise the risk of breathing depression and death with other depressants, citing two papers (a review of how to find information on their potency, and a study of prescribed benzodiazepines taken with opioids by people starting dialysis), and presents no comparison of its own. It also reports, from agency sources, counterfeit Xanax (alprazolam) tablets holding etizolam, flualprazolam or phenazepam seized in the US, Australia, Singapore and Malaysia, flubromazolam first identified in tablets labelled 'XANAX', seven young people treated in emergency departments after taking what they thought was alprazolam (flualprazolam, not confirmed in three), and products holding variable amounts or other drugs, generally without the buyer knowing. What drug checking found in pills and powders sold as something else is in the answers on fake pills and on benzodiazepine test strips. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Are designer benzos like etizolam more dangerous? Nobody has compared them with prescription benzos, and the reports below count only people who got into trouble, not everyone who used them. In 234 reports to US poison centres in 2014 to 2017 that named a designer benzo and no other drug, mostly etizolam, 65 in 100 people were drowsy, 4 in 100 were in a coma and 3 in 100 needed a breathing tube; of those whose care was recorded, 22 in 100 went to intensive care, and one man died. For 85 in 100 of those with a recorded duration, the effects were over within a day. Nobody tested in a laboratory which drug these people had really taken. In published reports of deaths up to 2021, gathered second-hand by a review, almost all involved other drugs as well: 115 of 141 death entries also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug; a few people seem to be listed twice. Reports to US poison centres rose from 26 to 112 a year, partly because new codes were added in 2016; etizolam alone went from 26 to 60. Designer benzos have also turned up in fake Xanax pills.
population: People reported to US poison centres after an intentional exposure to a single coded designer benzodiazepine, 2014–2017 (234 reports); people in published case reports and forensic series up to March 2021, as compiled in one review (141 death entries, 63 impaired drivers and 44 emergency admissions; Finland, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Sweden, the UK and the USA)
exposure: Designer benzodiazepines (mostly etizolam, clonazolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam), as named by callers and coded (poison centres) or found by forensic analysis (case reports), alone or with other drugs
comparator: None: no comparison with prescribed benzodiazepines or with people who used designer benzodiazepines without harm; within the review's table, death entries with and without other drugs (editors' count)
outcome: Clinical effects, treatments, level of care, graded outcome, duration and deaths coded by poison centres; deaths, impaired driving and emergency admissions in published reports, with the other drugs found
magnitude: Carpenter et al. (2019), NPDS 2014–2017: 474 exposures; 234 intentional single-agent exposures analysed (etizolam 162, clonazolam 50, flubromazolam 13, diclazepam 4, flubromazepam 3, meclonazepam 1, norflurazepam 1); per year 26, 30, 66, 112 (etizolam alone 26, 30, 46, 60; other agents coded only from 2016); median age 25 (13–63); men 86%; suspected suicide 42 (18%). Of 234: drowsiness/lethargy 152 (65%), slurred speech 40 (17%), confusion 32 (14%), agitated/irritable 22 (9%; text 14%), ataxia 21 (9%), tachycardia 20 (9%), hypotension 19 (8%), coma 10 (4%; text 8%), bradycardia 9 (4%); intubation 7 (3%). Disposition, 224 recorded (editors' sum): treated and released 92 (41%), non-critical admission 31 (14%), critical care 49 (22%), psychiatric facility 36 (16%), lost to follow-up or left 16 (7%). Outcome: major effect 9 (4%), death 1 (0.4%). Duration under 24 h 151 of 178 (84.8%, editors' sum; text 85%). No intervals; no laboratory confirmation. Brunetti et al. (2021), published reports to March 2021: 254 cases (141 deaths, 63 DUID, 44 ED, 3 outpatient, 2 self-administration, 1 drug offence); deaths phenazepam 60, flualprazolam 38, etizolam 34, flubromazolam 4, five others 1 each. Editors' count of the Table 1 death entries: any opioid 115 of 141 (81.6%; etizolam 29 of 34, flualprazolam 27 of 38, phenazepam 53 of 60, flubromazolam 3 of 4, others 3 of 5; methadone 51, morphine or 6-acetylmorphine 49), loperamide or its metabolite 2, no other substance 3; four apparent double entries, all with an opioid: 111 of 137 (81.0%) counting each once.

risk_of_bias.note: Poison-centre reports: the drug is the caller's report as coded, never confirmed in a laboratory; voluntary reporting favours people with symptoms; half of all reports (those with other substances) were excluded; codes changed in 2016; two percentages in the text contradict the table (card sc_carpenter_2019: JBI, moderate as a description, high as evidence of what a named drug does). Published cases: severe and detected cases, chosen by one author with no stated rule for judging contribution, not appraised, with some people apparently listed twice (card sc_brunetti_2021: high).

inconsistency.note: The two sources agree in direction: the reported effects are mostly sedation, and deaths without other drugs are rare in both (1 death among 234 single-substance poison-centre reports; 3 of 141 death entries in the review's table list no other drug).

indirectness.note: The deaths are known only through a review's compilation of case reports, which were not read (second-hand); the poison-centre data cover single-substance reports only, while most deaths involved other drugs; neither source compares designer with prescribed benzodiazepines, which is why the claim is worded as insufficient evidence for that comparison.

imprecision.note: Counts of reports; the one death among 234 single-substance reports is a single event, which the statement gives as a count.

publication_bias.note: The selection of published cases is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

grade.reasoning: Insufficient evidence for the comparison the question asks about: no source read compares designer with prescribed benzodiazepines, and neither has a count of the people who used them, so neither gives a risk per use. The descriptive findings start low (poison-centre records and case reports), are downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness (bounded at very low), and are never upgraded. Status replicated: two independent sources, a national US poison-centre series and a review of case reports from eight countries that does not include that series, agree in direction (mostly sedation; deaths without other drugs rare); each figure comes from one source, and the review cites the poison-centre study only for the point that many people exposed may have no serious effects. The share of death entries listing an opioid is the editors' count of the review's table (115 of 141; 111 of 137 counting each apparent double entry once), which the review itself does not give; it describes which drugs were found together in reported deaths, not whether the combination caused them.
